messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
We prove both directions by connecting the nested closed-set property with Cauchy sequences.
First, does completeness imply the intersection property?
Let (F_n) satisfy the hypotheses and choose x_n in F_n for each n.
Because m >= n puts both x_m and x_n in F_n, the shrinking diameters make x_n Cauchy.
Does completeness then supply a limit point?
Yes, completeness gives x in M with x_n -> x, and each closed F_k contains x_n for all n >= k.
Hence x belongs to every F_k, so the intersection is nonempty.
Conversely, does the intersection property imply completeness?
Take any Cauchy sequence y_n in M and define C_n as the closure of the tail {y_m : m >= n}.
The sets C_n are nonempty, closed, nested, and have diameters tending to zero because the Cauchy condition makes tail diameters tend to zero and closure does not increase diameter.
Does the property therefore produce a limit for y_n?
It gives x in all C_n, and for every k and m >= k we have d(x,y_m) <= diam C_k, so y_n -> x and M is complete.
